summary.text: The Catalan partial sum is transformed into a binomial convolution \(B_s(N)=\sum_i h_i\binom{sN}{N-i}\), where \(h_0=1\) and thereafter \(h_i\) is the period-three pattern \(2,-1,-1\) (with only a harmless additive constant in the exceptional parameter case).  Factoring \((1+X)^p-1-X^p=p(1+X+X^2)S(X)\) and expanding shows that the first two correction orders vanish by anti-palindromic symmetry, while for every higher order paired skew-binomial terms contribute the three factors \(M\), \(M(T-1)\), and \(M(T-2)\), and the bound \(v_p(\ell!)\le \ell-3\) lets the explicit \(p^\ell\) absorb the factorial denominator; Newton interpolation then extends the resulting \(p^{3e+3}\)-divisibility from nonnegative to arbitrary integer \(s\).

full_proof.text:
We prove the slightly stronger statement in which the exponent multiplier 4 is replaced by an arbitrary integer m. The conjecture for A333096 is then the case m=4.

Throughout, for an integer z and a nonnegative integer r, write

\[
 {z\choose r}=\frac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-r+1)}{r!}\in\mathbb Z,
\]

with \({z\choose0}=1\). This is the usual generalized binomial coefficient.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The Catalan coefficients and an auxiliary sequence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let

\[
c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}.
\]

It satisfies \(c(x)=1+xc(x)^2\). Lagrange inversion, applied after writing \(c=1+u\), gives, for every positive integer r,

\[
[x^j]c(x)^r=\frac{r}{r+j}{r+2j-1\choose j}
=\frac{r}{r+2j}{r+2j\choose j}.                 \tag{1}
\]

Thus, for positive n, the value at 1 of the degree-n Taylor truncation of \(c(x)^{mn}\) is

\[
a_m(n)=\sum_{j=0}^n \frac{mn}{mn+j}{mn+2j-1\choose j}.             \tag{2}
\]

For arbitrary integral m we interpret the summands by the same integral generalized-Catalan coefficient. In particular the coefficient with \(j=0\) is 1. This agrees with the ordinary Taylor coefficient when the latter is given by (1). We also set \(a_m(0)=1\).

We next introduce a periodic coefficient sequence

\[
h_0=1,
\qquad
h_i=\begin{cases}
2,&i>0\text{ and }3\mid i,\\
-1,&i>0\text{ and }3\nmid i.
\end{cases}                                      \tag{3}
\]

Its generating series is characterized by

\[
(1+x+x^2)\sum_{i\ge0}h_i x^i=1-x^2.              \tag{4}
\]

Indeed, the first coefficients are \(1,-1,-1,2,-1,-1,2,\ldots\), and from index 1 onward they have period 3; equivalently,

\[
h_{r+3}+h_{r+2}+h_{r+1}=0\qquad(r\ge0).          \tag{5}
\]

For an integer s and \(N\ge0\), define

\[
B_s(N)=\sum_{i=0}^N h_i {sN\choose N-i}.          \tag{6}
\]

The reason for this definition is the following identity.

**Lemma 1.** If \(N>0\) and \(m\ne-1\), then

\[
a_m(N)=B_{m+2}(N).                               \tag{7}
\]

If \(m=-1\), then

\[
a_{-1}(N)=B_1(N)+1.                              \tag{8}
\]

**Proof.** For \(j>0\), provided \(r+j\ne0\), the elementary binomial recurrence gives

\[
\frac r{r+j}{r+2j-1\choose j}
={r+2j-1\choose j}-{r+2j-1\choose j-1}.          \tag{9}
\]

Indeed, after multiplication by \(r+j\), this is equivalent to

\[
j{r+2j-1\choose j}=(r+j){r+2j-1\choose j-1},
\]

which is the standard adjacent-binomial identity.

We need the finite convolution identity

\[
\sum_{j=0}^N\left({r+2j-1\choose j}
-\mathbf1_{j>0}{r+2j-1\choose j-1}\right)
=
\sum_{i=0}^N h_i{r+2N\choose N-i}.                \tag{10}
\]

Here the summand at \(j=0\) on the left is 1. For completeness, (10) follows directly from Pascal's identity and (5). One convenient induction is to reflect the sum on the right and put

\[
R_N(x)=\sum_{j=0}^N h_{N-j}{x\choose j}.
\]

Twice applying Pascal's identity yields

\[
R_{N+1}(x+2)-R_N(x)
={x\choose N+1}-\mathbf1_{N>0}{x\choose N-1}.     \tag{11}
\]

All interior coefficients cancel because three consecutive h's sum to zero; at the lower boundary one uses
\(h_2+h_1+h_0=-1\), while the remaining two boundary terms are exactly those displayed in (11). Starting with \(R_0(x)=1\), summing (11) with \(x=r+2N\) proves (10).

Take \(r=mN\). If \(m\ne-1\), then \(mN+j\ne0\) for every \(1\le j\le N\): this is immediate for \(m\ge0\), while for \(m\le-2\), equality would imply \(j=(-m)N\ge2N>N\). Thus (9) applies term by term, and (10) gives

\[
a_m(N)=\sum_{i=0}^N h_i{mN+2N\choose N-i}=B_{m+2}(N).
\]

When \(m=-1\), (9) still applies for \(j<N\). At \(j=N\), the defining quotient has denominator zero and its integral-division value is 0. On the other hand, the corresponding difference in (10) is

\[
{N-1\choose N}-{N-1\choose N-1}=-1.
\]

Consequently deleting that last difference increases the sum by 1, proving (8). ∎

The main task is therefore the following prime-step divisibility statement.

**Proposition 2.** Let p be prime, \(p\ge5\), let \(M>0\), and suppose \(p^e\mid M\). Then, for every integer s,

\[
p^{3e+3}\mid B_s(pM)-B_s(M).                    \tag{12}
\]

Most of the proof is devoted to Proposition 2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. A scaled freshman quotient
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put

\[
D(x)=1+x+x^2,\qquad A(x)=1-x^2,
\]

and

\[
R_p(x)=(1+x)^p-1-x^p.
\]

We first prove that there is an integral polynomial S such that

\[
R_p(x)=pD(x)S(x).                                 \tag{13}
\]

First, \(D\mid R_p\). Modulo D one has \(x^3=1\) and \(1+x=-x^2\). Since a prime \(p\ge5\) is odd and is not divisible by 3, its residue modulo 3 is 1 or 2. Hence

\[
(1+x)^p\equiv(-x^2)^p=-x^{2p}\pmod D.
\]

If \(p\equiv1\pmod3\), then \(x^p\equiv x\) and \(x^{2p}\equiv x^2\); if \(p\equiv2\pmod3\), these two residues are interchanged. In either case

\[
-x^{2p}-1-x^p\equiv-(1+x+x^2)\equiv0\pmod D.
\]

Thus \(R_p=DT\) for some \(T\in\mathbb Z[x]\).

Every coefficient of \(R_p\) is divisible by p: the constant and degree-p coefficients vanish, and for \(0<r<p\) the coefficient is \({p\choose r}\), divisible by p. We now show every coefficient of T is divisible by p. If \(T=\sum t_rx^r\), then the coefficients of \(DT\) are

\[
t_0,\quad t_1+t_0,\quad t_r+t_{r-1}+t_{r-2}\quad(r\ge2).
\]

Induction on r, using the divisibility of the coefficients of \(DT=R_p\), gives \(p\mid t_r\) for all r. Therefore \(T=pS\) with \(S\in\mathbb Z[x]\), proving (13).

We also need the symmetry of S. Reflection of a polynomial about degree d means replacing its coefficient at r by its coefficient at \(d-r\). The polynomial \((1+x)^p\), and hence \(R_p\), is palindromic about degree p. The polynomial D is palindromic about degree 2. Since \(\deg R_p\le p\) and \(\deg D=2\), equation (13) implies

\[
\deg S\le p-2.                                   \tag{14}
\]

Reflecting (13) about degree p and cancelling the nonzero polynomial D and the nonzero scalar p shows

\[
S^*(x)=S(x),                                      \tag{15}
\]

where the reflection is about degree \(p-2\). Thus S is palindromic about degree \(p-2\). Also

\[
S(0)\text{ as a coefficient is }0,               \tag{16}
\]

because the constant coefficient of \(R_p\) is zero, whereas the constant coefficient of \(pDS\) is p times that of S.

For every \(l\ge1\), define

\[
P_l(x)=A(x)D(x)^{l-1}S(x)^l.                     \tag{17}
\]

The polynomial A is anti-palindromic about degree 2, while D is palindromic about degree 2 and S is palindromic about degree \(p-2\). Products and powers add reflection degrees. Consequently

\[
P_l^*(x)=-P_l(x)\quad\text{about degree }pl,      \tag{18}
\]

because

\[
2+2(l-1)+l(p-2)=pl.
\]

Moreover,

\[
\deg P_l\le pl,
\qquad [x^0]P_l=0.                               \tag{19}
\]

The second assertion follows from \(l\ge1\) and (16).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Expansion of \(B_T(pM)\) for a nonnegative integer T
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first prove (12) when the integer parameter s is a nonnegative integer \(T\ge2\).

From (13),

\[
(1+x)^p=1+x^p+pD(x)S(x).
\]

Raising this to the power MT gives

\[
(1+x)^{pMT}
=
\sum_{l=0}^{MT}{MT\choose l}
   (pDS)^l(1+x^p)^{MT-l}.                         \tag{20}
\]

Because \({T(pM)\choose pM-i}=[x^{pM-i}](1+x)^{pMT}\), inserting (20) into the definition of \(B_T(pM)\) expresses it as a sum of correction terms \(C_l\), \(0\le l\le MT\).

The term \(l=0\) is exactly \(B_T(M)\). To see this, extract only coefficients whose indices are multiples of p. Contraction by p changes \((1+x^p)^{MT}\) into \((1+x)^{MT}\). In addition,

\[
h_{pa}=h_a,                                      \tag{21}
\]

because \(p\ne3\), so multiplication by p preserves divisibility by 3 and preserves whether the index is zero. Thus the l=0 contribution contracts to

\[
\sum_{a=0}^M h_a{MT\choose M-a}=B_T(M).
\]

We now rewrite every positive-l correction. Identity (4) says that convolution by D changes the h-sequence into the coefficient sequence of A. Using one of the l factors D in \((pDS)^l\), and then extracting the coefficient at \(pM\), gives

\[
C_l=p^l\sum_{a=0}^l u_a{MT\choose l}\,
              \beta_a,                           \tag{22}
\]

where

\[
u_a=[x^{pa}]P_l(x),
\qquad
\beta_a=\begin{cases}
{MT-l\choose M-a},&a\le M,\\
0,&a>M.
\end{cases}                                      \tag{23}
\]

Here is the coefficient extraction behind (22). After cancellation of one D against the h-convolution, the remaining polynomial is \(P_l=A D^{l-1}S^l\). The coefficient supplied by \((1+x^p)^{MT-l}\) is \({MT-l\choose M-a}\). Because \(\deg P_l\le pl\), only \(0\le a\le l\) can occur. This proves (22).

By (18) and (19), the sampled sequence \(u_a=[x^{pa}]P_l\) satisfies

\[
u_{l-a}=-u_a\quad(0\le a\le l),
\qquad u_0=u_l=0.                                \tag{24}
\]

For \(l=1\), both sampled coefficients are endpoints and hence zero. For \(l=2\), the endpoints vanish and the middle coefficient equals its own negative, hence also vanishes. Therefore

\[
C_1=C_2=0.                                       \tag{25}
\]

It remains to prove the required divisibility for \(l\ge3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Pairing the anti-palindromic coefficients
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(l\ge3\), and pair a with \(j=l-a\). Put

\[
N=MT,
\qquad K=M(T-1),
\]

so \(N=M+K\), \(M\le K\), and

\[
p^e\mid M,
\qquad p^e\mid K,
\qquad p^e\mid K-M,                              \tag{26}
\]

because \(K=M(T-1)\) and \(K-M=M(T-2)\).

Define

\[
Y_i={N\choose l}(\beta_i-\beta_{l-i}).            \tag{27}
\]

Using (24), the inner sum in (22) becomes

\[
\sum_{0\le i<l-i}u_iY_i.                         \tag{28}
\]

The midpoint, if present, contributes zero, and the two endpoints vanish. Thus only pairs with \(i,j=l-i\) both positive matter.

We require a divisibility estimate for each \(p^lY_i\). The key exact identity is

\[
l!Y_i
={N\choose M}i!j!\left(
 {M\choose i}{K\choose j}-{M\choose j}{K\choose i}
\right),                                         \tag{29}
\]

where \(j=l-i\). This follows from the standard counting identity

\[
{N\choose M}{M\choose i}{K\choose j}
={N\choose l}{l\choose i}{N-l\choose M-i},       \tag{30}
\]

and the analogous identity with i and j interchanged, together with
\({l\choose i}i!j!=l!\). Formula (30) remains correct with the convention that an out-of-range binomial coefficient is zero.

We next record the elementary divisibility behind the right side of (29): provided i and j are positive and at most both M and K,

\[
MK(K-M)
\mid i!j!\left(
 {M\choose i}{K\choose j}-{M\choose j}{K\choose i}
\right).                                         \tag{31}
\]

To prove (31), write the descending factorial as

\[
n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)=nQ_r(n),
\qquad
Q_r(X)=\prod_{t=1}^{r-1}(X-t).
\]

The difference \(Q_r(K)-Q_r(M)\) is divisible by \(K-M\), since the difference of the values of any integral polynomial is divisible by the difference of its arguments. Hence

\[
Q_i(M)Q_j(K)-Q_j(M)Q_i(K)

tagsup{is divisible by }K-M.
\]

After multiplying by MK, this says that

\[
M^{\underline i}K^{\underline j}
-M^{\underline j}K^{\underline i}

tagsup{is divisible by }MK(K-M).
\]

Since \(n^{\underline r}=r!{n\choose r}\), this is exactly (31).

In a pair with \(i<j\) and \(j\le M\), all the bounds needed in (31) hold: \(i<j\le M\le K\). By (26),

\[
p^{3e}\mid MK(K-M),                              \tag{32}
\]

and therefore (29)-(31) imply

\[
p^{3e}\mid l!Y_i.                               \tag{33}
\]

We must clear the possible p-part of \(l!\). Legendre's estimate gives

\[
v_p(l!)\le \frac{l}{p-1}\le\frac l4\le l-3
\qquad(l\ge3,\,p\ge5).                          \tag{34}
\]

Combining (33) and (34),

\[
v_p(p^lY_i)
=l+v_p(Y_i)
\ge l+3e-v_p(l!)
\ge3e+3.
\]

Thus

\[
p^{3e+3}\mid p^lY_i.                            \tag{35}
\]

Multiplication by \(u_i\) and summation over all pairs preserves divisibility.

There is one harmless range issue: the preceding pair argument used \(j\le M\). If \(l\le M\), this is automatic. If \(M<l\), no pairing argument is needed. The leading factor \(p^l\) in (22) already supplies the desired power. Indeed, if \(e=0\), then \(3e+3=3\le l\). If \(e>0\), then \(p^e\le M<l\), and

\[
3e+3\le p^e+1\le l.                              \tag{36}
\]

The first inequality follows by induction from \(p\ge5\): for e=1 it is \(6\le6\), and exponential growth by a factor at least 5 dominates the increase by 3. Therefore again \(p^{3e+3}\mid p^l\).

We have proved that every correction \(C_l\) with \(l>0\) is divisible by \(p^{3e+3}\): for \(l=1,2\) it is zero, and for \(l\ge3\) this follows from (35) or (36). Since \(C_0=B_T(M)\), equation (20) now gives

\[
p^{3e+3}\mid B_T(pM)-B_T(M)\qquad(T\ge2).       \tag{37}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The two small nonnegative parameters
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(T=0\), generalized binomial coefficients give

\[
B_0(N)=h_N.
\]

By (21), \(h_{pM}=h_M\), so the difference is exactly zero.

For \(T=1\), symmetry of ordinary binomial coefficients gives

\[
B_1(N)=\sum_{j=0}^N h_j{N\choose j}.              \tag{38}
\]

Let more generally

\[
F_k(N)=\sum_{j=0}^N h_{j+k}{N\choose j}.
\]

Pascal's identity gives

\[
F_k(N+1)=F_k(N)+F_{k+1}(N).                       \tag{39}
\]

Using the three-term relation (5), including its initial boundary correction, one obtains

\[
F_1(N)+F_2(N)=-F_0(N)-1,
\]

and hence

\[
F_0(N+2)=F_0(N+1)-F_0(N)-1.                      \tag{40}
\]

Applying (40) repeatedly shows \(F_0(N+6)=F_0(N)\). Its six values are

\[
F_0(0),\ldots,F_0(5)=1,0,-2,-3,-2,0.             \tag{41}
\]

A prime \(p\ge5\) is congruent to 1 or 5 modulo 6. Multiplication by 1 clearly preserves the table (41), and multiplication by 5 negates residues modulo 6; the table is symmetric under \(r\mapsto-r\). Thus

\[
B_1(pM)=F_0(pM)=F_0(M)=B_1(M).                   \tag{42}
\]

Together, (37), the T=0 case, and (42) prove the prime-step congruence for every nonnegative integer parameter T.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Extension to every integer parameter
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For fixed N, \(B_s(N)\), regarded as a function of s, is an integer-valued polynomial of degree at most N, because each \({sN\choose N-i}\) is a polynomial in s of degree at most \(N-i\). Define its Newton coefficients

\[
C_r(N)=\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^{r-j}{r\choose j}B_j(N).  \tag{43}
\]

These are the r-th forward differences at zero. The Newton expansion is

\[
B_s(N)=\sum_{r=0}^N{s\choose r}C_r(N)             \tag{44}
\]

for every integer s. This is the standard Newton formula; it follows by repeated use of Pascal's identity, and terms above N vanish because the \((N+1)\)-st forward difference of a degree-at-most-N polynomial is zero.

For each nonnegative j, the already proved result says

\[
p^{3e+3}\mid B_j(pM)-B_j(M).
\]

Taking the integral linear combination (43) therefore gives, for every r,

\[
p^{3e+3}\mid C_r(pM)-C_r(M).                    \tag{45}
\]

In (44), expand \(B_s(pM)\) over \(0\le r\le pM\). Expand \(B_s(M)\) over the same range; this is legitimate because \(C_r(M)=0\) for \(r>M\). Subtracting and using (45) term by term yields

\[
p^{3e+3}\mid
\sum_{r=0}^{pM}{s\choose r}\bigl(C_r(pM)-C_r(M)\bigr)
=B_s(pM)-B_s(M).
\]

This proves Proposition 2 for every integer s.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Final specialization and the supercongruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(p\ge5\) be prime and let \(n,k>0\). Put

\[
M=n p^{k-1},\qquad e=k-1.
\]

Then \(M>0\), \(p^e\mid M\), and

\[
pM=np^k,
\qquad
3e+3=3(k-1)+3=3k.                                \tag{46}
\]

Applying Proposition 2 with \(s=m+2\) gives

\[
p^{3k}\mid B_{m+2}(np^k)-B_{m+2}(np^{k-1}).     \tag{47}
\]

If \(m\ne-1\), Lemma 1 turns (47) directly into

\[
a_m(np^k)\equiv a_m(np^{k-1})\pmod{p^{3k}}.      \tag{48}
\]

If \(m=-1\), Lemma 1 adds 1 to both B-values, so the same congruence follows as well. Hence (48) holds for every integer m.

Finally take \(m=4\). By (1)-(2), \(a_4(N)\) is exactly the value at \(x=1\) of the degree-N Taylor truncation of \(c(x)^{4N}\), namely A333096. Therefore, for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers n and k,

\[
\boxed{\ a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod{p^{3k}}\ }.
\]

This is the claimed supercongruence.
